edits.english: Ravina continued to inform Rav Pappa of Rava’s statements: Rava further raises another contradiction: Did Rav Yehuda say that Rav says that a sin offering that one slaughtered for the sake of a burnt offering is unfit, whereas if one slaughtered the sin offering for the sake of non-sacred meat, it is fit? Apparently, only improper intent that is of its type, i.e., for the sake of another offering, ruins the sin offering and renders it unfit, whereas wrong intent that is not of its type, i.e., for the sake of non-sacred meat, is disregarded and does not ruin the sin offering.
Rava further raises another contradiction - This refers to Ravina and Rav Pappa, who said that Rava raised contradictions between rulings and resolved them.
That Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav - This is stated later, in the chapter 'Beit Shammai' (Zevachim 46b).

It is fit if slaughtered for the sake of non-sacred meat - It entered our mind to say that this is his own reasoning, as he explains, that something of its own type is effective in uprooting its name.

That is not of its type - For example, non-sacred animals, which are not a type of consecrated offering. It does not ruin it, and its name is not applied to the sin offering to uproot its original name from it.

The Rambam rules that although a Pesach offering is similar to a sin offering in that both are disqualified if they are slaughtered for the sake of the wrong offering, a Pesach offering that is slaughtered for the sake of non-sacred meat is disqualified, whereas a sin offering is not. This ruling is derived in the Jerusalem Talmud from the verse: “It is the offering of the Lord’s Passover” (Exodus 12:27). The Rambam also writes that in a case where a sin offering was slaughtered for the sake of non-sacred meat, although the sin offering is fit, it does not satisfy the obligation of its owner. The Ramban (Milĥamot HaShem on tractate Rosh HaShana) maintains that it does satisfy the obligation of the owner (see Rambam’s Commentary on the Mishna, and Sefer Avoda, Hilkhot Pesulei HaMukdashin 15:11).

However, it did not satisfy the owner's obligation (Rambam). But the Ramban (in Milchamot HaShem on Tractate Rosh HaShana) holds that in a case where one slaughtered a sin offering for the sake of non-sacred meat, it did satisfy the owner's obligation.

For something that is not of its type at all, such as non-sacred animals in relation to consecrated offerings, is not considered something that can be attached to it in order to uproot the name of the sin offering from it (Rashi).

Later authorities wrote (see in Chazon Yechezkel and elsewhere) that from here it is proven that the primary disqualification when one changes its name from one sacred offering to another is not on the negative side, by uprooting its previous name, but on the positive side—that one designates this offering for another purpose. And therefore, it does not have the power to designate the purpose of a sin offering that was consecrated for the sake of non-sacred animals, which are not of its type at all.

A sin offering that was slaughtered for the sake of another offering (such as a burnt offering) — this is disqualified. But if one slaughtered it for the sake of non-sacred animals — this is fit, but it did not satisfy the owner's obligation. In accordance with Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav. (Rambam Sefer Avoda Hilkhot Pesulei HaMukdashin 15:4).
